transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Giles Snyder.
President Trump says he wouldn't mind if Jensen Huang returned as NVIDIA's CEO.
NPR's Franco Ordonez reports that Trump says he thinks Huang learned a big lesson.
Jensen Huang stepped down last week following allegations of multiple extramarital affairs,
including one with a suspected Chinese spy.
President Trump said national security, though, was never at risk because of the affairs
and questioned whether the woman involved was actually a spy.
I don't know that she is a spy.
Usually what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country,
that's a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she's a spy.
I don't know that she was a spy at all.
The president also dismissed reports that he was told by intelligence
showing that Huang was in a relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy.
Franco Ordonez and PR News, the White House.
President Trump is now on his way to Asia.
He's due to make a stop in the Philippines Tuesday before traveling on to China,
where he is to meet with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
Trump said Monday he may also meet with North Korea's Kim Jong-un.
United Airlines says the tech outage at delayed departures today has been resolved
and that there are no indications of a cyber security issue.
Officials believe United's outage is not connected to Friday's air traffic control outage
that led the FAA to ground planes nationwide on Friday.
And PR's Joel Rose says that outage is under investigation.
The exact details are still under investigation,
but there were some warnings about exactly this scenario
in a report that was released just in September by the General Accountability Office.
The GAO report noted that the administration has been speeding up the timeline
of modernization work that was already underway,
including on this exact telecommunications network that apparently failed on Friday.
The foreign ministers of Australia, Canada, Italy and the UK urging Israel
to allow more humanitarian supplies into Gaza.
They warn that 150,000 tents and other essential items are being held at the border
as winter sets in. Here's NPR's Anas Baba reporting.
The first major winter storm has already flooded displacement camps across Gaza,
leaving thousands of families exposed to more rain and cold.
Yam Egeland, head of the Norwegian Refugee Council, says
the world has normalized Palestinian suffering.
Humanitarian agencies, he says, have been reduced to big ink for the bare minimum.
"We find ourselves big in even for tents," he says.
And instead of proper housing, materials and heating,
Egeland says aid groups are bleeding for blankets.
Israel says it has plans in place to address Gaza's needs ahead of winter.
But aid agencies say restrictions on essential supplies
are leaving millions of Palestinians vulnerable to the coming month.
Anas Baba and Fair News, Gaza City.
This is NPR.
JPMorgan Chase is blaming a software bug
that caused problems throughout the financial system today.
But Chase says the problem was an isolated incident
and not the result of a cyber attack.
The tech issue resulted in thousands of customers
reporting difficulty accessing online accounts
as well as several major U.S. banks and the money transfer service sell.
The National Transportation Safety Board says it plans to issue a preliminary report
within a month on Friday's collision between a tanker
and a smaller river cruise ship docked in New Orleans.
The collision sent dozens of people into the water.
190 passengers and crew on the cruise ship survived.
Officials say no one suffered critical injuries
before it remained hospitalized Monday.
A new feature film tells the story of Judy Heumann,
a wheelchair user who in 1977 helped lead
a month-long sit-in of a federal building to demand change.
And Piers Janakimeta reports.
"The federal government cannot steal our civil rights."
The new movie, Being Human, is about how a band of activists
made the government enforce its first civil rights law
for people with disabilities.
Now, 50 years since that battle was won, it's being fought again.
And it is our job to carry on her legacy
and keep that fire burning all these decades later.
That's 23-year-old disability rights activist Kaylee Brendel
who runs an organization called Judy's League.
She started it to push back against the Trump administration's efforts
to back the very protections Judy Heumann helped win.
She says watching the film gave her new resolve
and reminded her this battle had been won once before.
This is NPR News.

topics.text: President Trump says he wouldn't mind if Jensen Huang returned as NVIDIA CEO after affair allegations
Trump questions whether woman in Huang affair is a Chinese spy, dismisses intelligence reports
Trump heads to Asia, with stops in the Philippines and China to meet Xi Jinping and Putin
United Airlines says tech outage resolved, denies cybersecurity issue behind delayed departures
Officials say United outage unconnected to Friday's FAA air traffic control outage that grounded flights
Foreign ministers of Australia, Canada, Italy and UK urge Israel to allow more aid into Gaza
Winter storm floods Gaza displacement camps as aid agencies cite blocked tents and supplies
JPMorgan Chase blames software bug for widespread online banking disruptions, rules out cyberattack
NTSB to issue preliminary report within a month on New Orleans tanker and river cruise collision
New film Being Human tells story of Judy Heumann's 1977 sit-in for disability rights
